flawed_step: Step 3: the claim that the shortest interval g conflicts with at most one interval of an optimal schedule O is unjustified. A short interval can overlap the end of one interval and the start of the next, so swapping it in can lose two intervals of O.
counterexample: Intervals A=[0,10), B=[9,12), C=[11,22), with durations 10, 3 and 11 (all distinct). Greedy picks B, the shortest. B meets A on [9,10) and C on [11,12), so both are discarded and greedy returns 1 interval. {A,C} is a valid schedule because A and C do not intersect, so the optimum is at least 2. Since all durations differ, this happens under every tie-breaking rule.
assessment_summary:
Proof attempt (an exchange argument, with a per-step judgement):
1. Let g be the first interval greedy picks, i.e. the shortest one, and let O be an optimal schedule. — Justified: this is just setup.
2. If g is in O, induct on the intervals that do not conflict with g. — Justified: standard reduction.
3. If g is not in O, claim g conflicts with at most one member of O, because g is shortest. — NOT justified. Two members of O can be disjoint and still each intersect g: one ends inside g and the other starts inside g. Being shortest does not rule this out.
4. Swap: O' = O minus the conflicting member, plus g, so |O'| = |O|. — Not justified: it depends on step 3. If g conflicts with two members, |O'| = |O| - 1.
5. So some optimal schedule contains g, and the induction from step 2 finishes the proof. — Not justified: it depends on step 4.

Step 3 is not just a gap in this proof; the statement itself is false. Take A=[0,10), B=[9,12), C=[11,22), with durations 10, 3 and 11, all distinct. Greedy picks B first. B intersects A (on [9,10)) and C (on [11,12)), so both are removed and greedy ends with 1 interval. A and C are disjoint, so the optimum is 2. The durations are distinct, so tie-breaking plays no role. Greedy returns a strictly smaller schedule than the optimum, as the definitions require. Verdict: INVALID; the statement is false.
